stem: In simple linear regression y = b0 + b1·x, how is b1 estimated?

options.text: Covariance of x and y divided by the variance of x
Mean of y minus mean of x
Sum of y divided by sum of x

explanation: b1 = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) / Σ(x − x̄)²; then b0 = ȳ − b1·x̄.

stem: Squaring errors in the squared error loss removes negative signs and makes large errors count more.
explanation: That is why the squared error loss is used.

stem: What does gradient descent do to each parameter at every step?

options.text: Moves it in the opposite direction of the gradient, scaled by the learning rate
Moves it in the direction of the gradient

explanation: new weight = old weight − learning rate × gradient.

stem: What happens if the learning rate is too large?

options.text: The steps overshoot the minimum and may bounce or diverge
Training becomes extremely slow but stable
The model always reaches the exact minimum

explanation: A large learning rate can jump past the minimum; a small one is slow; zero never moves.

stem: Which are strategies of gradient descent?
explanation: Batch, stochastic and mini-batch are the three strategies.

stem: Which gradient descent strategy updates the parameters after every single training example?
explanation: SGD updates after each example: fast but noisy.

stem: Which one is not part of the gradient descent pseudocode in the course?

options.text: Compute the gradient of the cost

explanation: One-hot encoding is a feature engineering step, not part of gradient descent.

stem: Mini-batch gradient descent is used by almost every deep learning model because it is both fast and stable.
explanation: It combines the speed of SGD with the stability of batch updates.
